title: The Gene Test That Decides Which Breast Cancer Drug You Get
hook: One in five breast cancers is driven by an overactive gene called ERBB2 (HER2) — and a genetic test of the tumor, not the patient, now decides whether a targeted antibody drug will work.
key_points: The ERBB2 gene (also called HER2) is overexpressed in 15–20% of breast cancers, making tumors grow faster and historically carry a worse prognosis.
Trastuzumab (Herceptin) was the first monoclonal antibody built to target the HER2 receptor directly, and it improved outcomes when added to treatment.
Pertuzumab (Perjeta), a related antibody, is often combined with trastuzumab to further boost progression-free and overall survival.
Both drugs only work in HER2-positive tumors — every newly diagnosed breast cancer patient must have a validated HER2 test before treatment.
It's a landmark example of precision oncology: the drug prescribed depends on a molecular test of the tumor itself, not just the cancer's location or stage.
content_html: Not all breast cancer is the same at the molecular level, and treatment increasingly reflects that. In 15–20% of cases, tumor cells overexpress a receptor made by the ERBB2 gene, better known as HER2 — and that single genetic fact changes what drug gets prescribed.
extra_html: Trastuzumab (Herceptin) was the first monoclonal antibody engineered to target the HER2 receptor directly, and adding it to treatment measurably improved outcomes for HER2-positive breast and gastric cancers, historically among the faster-growing, worse-prognosis subtypes. A related antibody, pertuzumab (Perjeta), is now frequently combined with trastuzumab and chemotherapy — in advanced, neoadjuvant, and adjuvant settings alike — to push progression-free and overall survival even higher. Neither drug works without the right target: FDA labeling restricts both to patients whose tumors test positive for HER2 protein overexpression or ERBB2 gene amplification on a validated assay, which is why oncology guidelines require a HER2 test on every newly diagnosed breast cancer, and again on the tumor itself if the cancer later spreads. It's one of the clearest examples in medicine of a treatment decision driven entirely by a molecular test of the tumor rather than guesswork.

related.title: Why One Drug Dose Doesn't Fit All
related.hook: The blood thinner warfarin can need up to a 20-fold different dose from person to person — and about half of that swing is written into two of your genes.

related.title: How Genes Become Traits
related.hook: You inherit two copies of every gene — one from each parent — and the way those copies interact helps decide everything from eye color to blood type.

related.title: Cancer: When Cells Divide Wrong
related.hook: Cancer is cell division gone unchecked — a cell ignores the body's stop signals, multiplies relentlessly, and crowds out healthy tissue.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean for a breast cancer to be 'HER2-positive'?
flashcards.back_html: Its cells overexpress the receptor made by the ERBB2 (HER2) gene, which drives faster tumor growth. It affects 15–20% of breast cancers and determines whether HER2-targeted antibody drugs will work.

flashcards.prompt: How do trastuzumab and pertuzumab work against HER2-positive cancer?

choices.text: They're monoclonal antibodies that directly target the HER2 receptor on tumor cells
They edit the ERBB2 gene to delete it from tumor cells
They work by lowering the patient's overall immune response

flashcards.explanation_html: Both are monoclonal antibodies engineered to bind the HER2 (ERBB2) receptor; pertuzumab is often combined with trastuzumab for an even stronger effect.

flashcards.prompt: Why must every newly diagnosed breast cancer patient get a HER2 test before choosing treatment?

choices.text: HER2-targeted drugs only benefit patients whose tumors are confirmed HER2-positive
The test is required by law but has no effect on treatment choice
It measures how far the cancer has spread, not the drug's target

flashcards.explanation_html: Trastuzumab and pertuzumab are FDA-approved only for patients whose tumors test positive for HER2 protein overexpression or ERBB2 gene amplification, so the test directly determines eligibility for these therapies.
